Title: Passage 2: A Seal in the Making
Content: The Great Seal of the United States is a symbol of power and authority as a nation. It is seen throughout the rooms of the White House, on passports, and on U.S. `text(one-dollar)` bills. But how did the idea of the seal come to life? It wasn’t a quick and simple process.

Congress wanted an emblem that showed the power and authority of the United States. It needed to reflect the freedom of the people and the high hopes for the future of the country. The `text(first)` committee had the challenge of finding a way to translate these ideas into an image. Some ideas worked well, but ultimately it left Congress feeling unsatisfied.

With the `text(first)` committee failing, it was back to the drawing board. In `text(March 1780)`, a new committee was formed. Francis Hopkinson, the man who designed the American flag, was asked to serve as a guide while making a new design.

Influenced by the American flag, Hopkinson’s committee added `13` red and white stripes symbolizing the `13` colonies. A `ultext(constellation)` of `text(13 six-pointed)` stars and an olive branch, a symbol of peace, were part of the design. While these features are part of the final seal, Congress still declined the committee’s idea.

After `text(two)` failed designs, Congress appointed a `text(third)` committee with high hopes of being successful. This committee relied heavily on William Barton, an artistic lawyer, to nail this design. Barton’s committee added a small white eagle spreading its wings, a small flag, and a pyramid to the previous design. In May `1782`, he drew up `text(two)` designs, but Congress still rejected both ideas.

Congress decided to present the works of the `text(three)` committees to the Secretary of Congress, Charles Thomson. Though not an artist, he could make tough decisions. He chose the best features from the previous design and got to work.

He replaced the former white eagle with the native American bald eagle. Its wings were extended, and a small flag was added. The bird’s left talon held a bundle of arrows, and the right talon held an olive branch. Changes were made to the placement of other features too. Then, the rough sketches were given back to Barton for the final touches.

Barton made a simpler version of Thomson’s flag and alternated the white and red vertical stripes. He made it clear that the number of arrows in the eagle’s talon numbered `13`. The eagle’s wing tips also were turned upward.

The design was sent back to Thomson on `text(June 19, 1782)`, and he then added a written description of the seal with explanations for the changes. The final product was presented to Congress on `text(June 20)`. Finally, after `text(six years)` and the combined efforts of `14` men, Charles Thomson and William Barton were deemed successful when Congress approved this design.

`ultext(constellation)`: a group of stars that appear as a pattern or picture
